title: Slim Your Docker Images: Multi-Stage Diet 🐳
ig_caption:
From 865MB to 45MB… same app. Why does multi-stage cut the fat? 🔥

• Single-stage build = you ship the whole toolbox (including build tools, caches, and deps)
• That bigger image inherits more surface area → more potential vulnerabilities
• Multi-stage build = build in one stage, then copy only the runtime output into a fresh stage
• Result: smaller image size (865MB → 45MB) and fewer known CVEs (142 → 6)
• Less to scan, less to patch, faster pull/start, and better supply-chain hygiene

Production takeaway: Use multi-stage Dockerfiles with a minimal runtime base and copy only artifacts you need (e.g., binaries, static assets, installed production deps).

What’s your biggest “image diet” win—smaller size, fewer CVEs, or faster deployments? 👇
fb_caption:
Docker Image Diet (Multi-Stage) isn’t just about aesthetics—it’s an architectural boundary between “build” and “run.”

Trade-off behind the numbers (865MB → 45MB, 142 CVEs → 6):
- Single-stage images bake build tooling, intermediate dependencies, and caches into the final artifact.
- That increases the runtime attack surface, scanning results, and the amount of patch churn required when upstream components change.
- Multi-stage builds let you compile/package in an isolated builder stage, then copy only the final runtime artifacts into a separate, minimal runtime stage.

What happens under the hood:
- Stage 1 (builder): dependencies + compilers + build-time libraries live here. Their presence does not matter after the stage finishes.
- Stage 2 (runtime): starts from a clean image (often distroless or a slim base) and receives only what the application needs to execute.
- Final image contains the app only—so fewer packages means fewer known CVEs, fewer layers to maintain, and a smaller blast radius.

Scalability & resilience impacts:
- Faster distribution: smaller images reduce registry egress and node pull time, improving rollout speed.
- Lower operational overhead: fewer packages mean fewer updates, fewer breaking changes from unrelated tooling, and less time spent on vulnerability management.
- More predictable deployments: a runtime stage that contains only required artifacts reduces “it worked in build but not in run” drift.

Production best practice:
- Treat your runtime stage like production code: minimal base image, deterministic artifact copy, and avoid carrying build caches/tools into the final stage.
- Pair multi-stage builds with SBOM generation and automated image scanning so the “diet” is measurable and enforced.

Question: Are you optimizing for security (fewer CVEs), speed (smaller pulls), or cost (registry/egress)—and which one is winning for your workloads?
threads_caption: Single-stage ships the toolbox. Multi-stage ships the app. Same software, radically smaller image + fewer CVEs. Which do you prioritize first: speed, cost, or security? 🐳
